newsitem.title: CANADA: Toronto bourse embarrassed by computer crashes.
newsitem.headline: Toronto bourse embarrassed by computer crashes.

text.p: Plagued by a rash of computer crashes caused by frenzied trading in shares of Bre-X Minerals Ltd., the Toronto Stock Exchange is struggling to update its antiquated technology before its reputation is seriously tarnished.

Canada's largest equity market was embarrassed for the third time in as many sessions on Thursday when it was forced to halt trading again in shares of the troubled exploration company because of "technical difficulties."

A backlog of Bre-X trading orders crashed the TSE's entire computer trading system three times in the past week. Bre-X's shares in that period have been unavailable for trading on the exchange more often than they have traded.
The TSE was the butt of jokes on the U.S. financial news television channel CNBC on Wednesday, and irritated traders said the technical problems hurt the TSE's credibility.
"It's a huge black mark for Toronto to not be able to handle the volume in one stock. It's a joke, their computer system," said one trader.
The red-faced exchange was tinkering with its trading rules to try to reduce the number of unfilled orders sitting in the electronic order books.
But the effort had met with limited success.
On Wednesday and Thursday, the TSE was forced to lower the boom on trading in Bre-X in the middle of the session for fear that the crushing volume would drag down the whole exchange.

Bre-X has traded for only a few hours at a time in Toronto since it admitted last week it may have overstated its Busang dold discovery in Indonesia. But it attracted frantic interest each time it opened for trade.
The bourse's 20-year-old CATS (Computer Assisted Trading System) is in the process of being replaced by a system driven by TOREX trading engines supplied by the Paris Bourse.
But some market players have given up on CATS and are trading the old-fashioned way.
Frank Calta, director of trading at Anvil Institutional Services in New York, said he would keep an open telephone line to a floor trader in Toronto if he needed to trade Bre-X, avoiding the CATS.
Toronto-based VERSUS Brokerage Services was offering special crossing sessions on the Canadian Call network for Bre-X stock, matching trades from Toronto with other exchanges.
Bre-X shares have continued to trade in lighter volumes on the Nasdaq, Calgary, Alberta and Montreal exchanges.

The smaller Canadian exchanges, always considered the poor cousins of the TSE, are taking no small pride in their smooth trading of Bre-X. While the TSE was forced on Thursday to announce its trading of Bre-X was stopped once again, the Montreal Exchange issued news releases stating that trading continued there without a hitch.
Compounding the stress on the TSE's computer system is the migration of many stocks to computer trading from floor trading. All floor trading at the exchange is slated to close by the end of April.

More than 1,400 issues have already graduated to the CATS system, but many of Canada's most heavily traded stocks, including bank stocks and BCE Inc., Canada's largest publicly traded company, are still traded on the floor.
The migration of more stocks to the CATS system was put on hold while the exchange looked for a solution to the recent capacity problems.

Paul Bates, president of Porthmeor Securities Inc. and a TSE governor, said the system problems would be solved when the its new TOREX computer trading system took over by the end of 1997. Meanwhile, the TSE would try to adjust trading rules without compromising the fairness and flow of trading.

"The difficulty is you've got to be very, very careful because there's a sort of an equilibrium in the process and if you put one restriction in place you (might) in fact create another problem," Bates said.
